newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Russian FM sees no Syrian attack on Israel.
newsitem.headline: Russian FM sees no Syrian attack on Israel.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Thursday he did not think Syria was preparing a military strike against Israel and that his country would not support such aggression.
Primakov spoke to reporters in Tel Aviv after briefing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about his talks with Arab leaders.
"While being in Damascus, and I told the prime minister, I had no impression that the Syrians were preparing any strike against Israel," said Primakov.
"Russia is not going to support any party that uses force," he said. Primakov arrived in Israel after holding talks with Syrian, Lebanese and Egyptian leaders.
A Syrian redeployment of some 12,000 troops in Lebanon last month to within striking distance of a key Israeli position on the Golan Heights had given Israelis war jitters.
"I hope that impression reflects the situation," Netanyahu said about Primakov's remarks.
Netanyahu on Wednesday welcomed Syria's declaration this week it had no intentions of starting a war with the Jewish state.
Five years of peace talks between the two countries are stuck over the fate of the Golan Heights, captured by Israel from Syria in the 1967 Middle East war.
Earlier on Thursday, Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said he received important information from Primakov but declined to elaborate.
"I was able to receive impressions and very important information from his visit to our neighbouring countries," Levy told a joint news conference after they met.
Israel Radio said Primakov had brought a reassuring message from Damascus and wired a similar message from Israel to Syria after his meeting with Levy.
Asked if the situation with Damascus had calmed down, Levy said: "We are working on this matter."

Primakov said he welcomed Levy's recommitment to stick to agreements Israel signed with the Arabs. In Egypt on Wednesday, he had warned Israel it risked an outburst of violence if it tried to renegotiate peace deals with the PLO.

For more than three weeks Israel and the Palestinians have tried to salvage the peace process snagged on Hebron. Israel demands security guarantees for the 400 Jews who live and study in the centre of the town among 100,000 Arabs.

Israeli and Palestinian negotiators met late on Thursday for Primakov -- whose country was a co-sponsor of the 1991 Madrid peace summit that launched Arab-Israeli peace talks -- signed an agreement with Levy transferring former Soviet property in Israel to Russia.
